title: Freud in the Age of Therapy-Speak
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/anna-ballan
text:
W.H. Auden’s remark that Freud had become “a whole climate of opinion/under whom we conduct our different lives” has become something of a commonplace, but today it holds true only partially. We are all, in Philip Rieff’s lexicon, psychological men: We speak of triggers, defenses, attachment styles, and unconscious motives with a fluency that would have startled Freud’s most jargon-happy disciples.

But while the language we use is ostensibly analytic, our worldview is something like the inverse. Freud, read against the assumptions of our own therapeutic times, becomes uncooperative. The psychological culture popularized on screens often assumes several things: that you actually want to get better; that insight leads frictionlessly to change; that naming an issue defuses it; that the self is a project to be perfected. Freud assumes that a part of you—perhaps the most salient part—does not want to get better; that apparent insight can deepen the problem and naming an issue can intensify its grip; that the self is a kind of battlefield. If the therapy of today’s screen culture holds a mirror up to a curated self-image, actual therapy, Freud would insist, is more like a light held up over a swamp. 

Freud’s influence in the United States reached its peak in the 1950s through the 1970s, when he became an unquestioned sovereign of American intellectual and cultural life. Between the arrival of Freudian émigrés and the publication of new, authoritative translations—not to mention propagation by Erich Fromm, Erik Erikson, and others—Freud’s ideas took the college curriculum and popular imagination by storm. One need only watch early Woody Allen films to see the analyst treated as a kind of oracle, spoken of with the reverence one would ordinarily reserve for a sage or a rabbi. By the 1980s and 1990s, however, Freud had been effectively dethroned from his mid-century prestige. The rise of psychopharmacology, beloved by insurance companies for its cost-effectiveness, combined with the comparative efficiency of approaches such as cognitive behavioral therapy, started to eclipse the slow and narrative-based art of analysis. Not that these forms of treatment need be pitted against one another—each has its place, and they can work in tandem—but the overall trend was decisive: The American mind turned toward the quantifiable quicker fix. Psychoanalysis largely retreated into private practice and the academic humanities, and Freud himself was thrown out with the bath water—his blind spots and failures fairly taken to task, and his more outré flights of theory met with groans rather than knowing smiles.

The language of pop psychology, meanwhile, continued its absorption into the mainstream. Therapy found its way onto daytime television and bestseller lists; Oprah, Dr. Phil, and the self-help industry translated clinical concepts into everyday language. The burgeoning wellness industry coupled psychology with consumerism, while some corporate HR departments adopted their own therapeutic dialect (all the better to cushion mass layoffs). By the 2010s, Tumblr and other social-media platforms had made psychological vocabulary a kind of lingua franca, if only for an expanding cohort of plugged-in users. Even as the diffusion of that vocabulary brought clarity or relief to many—a point not to be minimized—for young people especially it seemed to dissolve into an insight-devouring churn, a talking-about-feelings rather than a working-through-them. Therapy-speak had been gaining ground, but the Freudian strand of it, with its attention to ambivalence, defenses, and drives, had been gradually sidelined. In its place arose a thinner idiom, one that promised empowerment through perpetual scrolling and self-disclosure rather than a plunge into the murkier depths of psychic life.

The False Promise of Self-Articulation

From a psychoanalytic perspective, the assumption that self-articulation liberates is only half true. The more articulate we are, the more elaborate and agile our evasions may become. Pathological symptoms are not random errors, after all: they are solutions the psyche has devised, protective compromises that maintain a precarious psychic equilibrium—a panic symptom that holds in abeyance a deeper grief, a chronic independence that protects against the anxiety of dependency, a rigid scruple that helps fend off an inconvenient desire. To unravel these is to tamper with a system that may, however painfully, be functioning. And naming a feeling—far from resolving it—can make it more dangerous, like a virus mutating under pressure. Freud noticed that his patients did something interesting. They claimed that they wanted to change, but they evolved intricate psychological ecosystems to ensure precisely that they didn’t, and they enlisted Freud as an accomplice in their stasis. 

What Freud experienced with his patients—the enlistment in their stasis—is an ever-present risk of therapy, and often the essence of bad therapy (though by no means the only way it can fail). At its worst, therapy can encourage confession without transformation, goading us along in our desire to be understood—but only half understood, understood through the flattering haze of a selectively edited narrative. Fifteen-second “therapy lessons” packaged like lifestyle content are grotesque caricatures of bad therapy, if the two can even be mentioned in the same breath. Freud sensed that our accounts of ourselves harden quickly into defenses. Videos with titles like “Twelve Signs Your Ex Was a Covert Narcissist,” or whatever the trending variant may be, cry out for analysis themselves; they are structurally incapable of challenging the viewer’s defenses and instead readily affirm them. Likewise, the “therapist reacts” genre of YouTube clips encourages the illusion that strangers can perform clinical interpretation in real time to audience applause.

Casual self-diagnosis flourishes as a consequence of such infotainment. Freud dismissed the idea that making the unconscious conscious could be accomplished by simply reciting traumatic childhood episodes or diagnostic labels at a patient: “Such measures,” he wrote in a 1910 essay, “have as much influence on the symptoms of nervous illness as a distribution of menu-cards in a time of famine has upon hunger.” Online, where self-description can be taken at face value, Freud’s suspicion of people’s self-assessments—his conviction that we deceive ourselves with spirited devotion—can feel hostile or plain unintelligible. Sándor Ferenczi’s remark that “the patient is not cured by free-associating, he is cured when he can free-associate” is instructive here. If analysis seeks to loosen the self-protective narratives people use to explain themselves, then the online self—shielded by a set of self-selected diagnostic terms—moves toward the opposite pole. Yet beneath any misapplied label lies the reality of human suffering: the apparent near ubiquity of anxiety, depression, and loneliness. Grasping at the diagnostic category du jour may be misguided, but the desperation driving it is authentic. You can no more reproach someone for it than you can blame a starving person for eyeing a menu; they are both looking for sustenance, however illusory it may prove. 

In this light, the so-called “triumph of the therapeutic” poses problems for therapy itself, and perhaps for the broader epidemic of unhappiness. The issue is not, as critics of therapy culture sometimes claim, too much self-awareness. It is, instead, a mixture of excessive awareness and insufficient awareness—yielding one might say the wrong kind of awareness, a state in which verbosity about the self coexists with a persistent style of self-evasion. In Freud’s time, psychological language was obscure and provocative; now it is democratized and inescapable. The vocabulary has become, in many cases, an easy way out. Our fluency in it has the capacity to deaden us. It follows, then, that successful therapy today has new work to do: It must sidestep not only the patient’s ordinary defenses but also the newer and more sophisticated defenses supplied by psychological jargon itself. The “talking cure” must become, against the odds, a way of hearing what all that talk is eminently capable of concealing. The miracle of good therapy, when it happens, is that the instrument of clarity and instrument of obfuscation are one and the same, and that the two can be made to diverge long enough for something real to break through—a feat not easily achieved without a therapist of rare skill and a patient of rare commitment.

The habit of drowning in words and getting crippled by thought predates Freud, of course. Shakespeare gives us Hamlet, talking himself in circles, reasoning himself into both feeling and action, sinking under the weight of self-interpretation (“What we think of as Freudian psychology is really a Shakespearean invention,” injects Harold Bloom with signature bardolatry, “and, for the most part, Freud is merely codifying it”). Anne Elliot, in Persuasion, thinks her way into paralysis. Dostoevsky’s Underground Man offers up torrents of self-analysis to little avail. Freud, for his part, understood himself as interpreting patterns latent in the human condition. Even Sappho cries, “my tongue is broken,” suggesting that this particular word-addled style of inwardness did not begin with some amorphous deity called “modernity.” What has changed is the scale. We inhabit a world where the tendencies Hamlet embodied are magnified, and where opportunities for self-commentary are effectively continuous.

Indeed, for all our talk of stress responses and maladaptive patterns, we have trouble naming the largest and most obvious source of contemporary psychic strain: our phones. A Freudian observer might take a look at our therapy-saturated culture and ask the obvious question: How is it that we are most fluent in therapeutic vocabulary at just the moment we are most ensnared in the psychic perils of social media? How can we talk about our symptoms with such confidence and exhibit so little insight into them? What is endless scrolling if not repetition compulsion—the drive to reenact what injures us—and the entire digital ecosystem if not a communal indulgence in neurosis? The irony is almost too on the nose: We narrate ourselves incessantly as we sink further and further into a trap of our own devising. The hyper-articulate patient doth protest too much. 

In a genuinely Freudian sense, the distress produced by our technological environment becomes the one thing we cannot see—or discuss without provoking yawns at best and accusations of Luddism at worst. The repression is collective and astonishingly effective. We broadcast our pain obsessively, clinging defensively to the device that exacerbates it, circulating the language of pop psychology through that same device. If Freud teaches us anything, it is that human beings express themselves through grand ironies. He did not himself conjure up this state of affairs; better to think him a kind of modern tragedian, a careful observer standing in suspicion of forces he is said to have unleashed. It is worth noting that one of his bolder speculations, the death instinct, is essentially inadmissible in a psychologized screen culture marked by mood trackers and optimization language. Freud’s account is tragic in the strict sense, as an account of human striving that includes its undoing and that sets the horizons of life modestly low. The language of optimization, with its model of the self as an engine of limitless upward striving, could scarcely be further from this account. 

The Father Withholds

Freud offers us little by way of consolation. “I have not the courage to rise up before my fellow-men as a prophet,” he avows at the end of Civilization and Its Discontents, “and I bow to their reproach that I can offer them no consolation: for at bottom, that is what they are all demanding—the wildest revolutionaries no less passionately than the most virtuous believers.” Freud’s stance is closer to one of tragic optimism, as his admirer Viktor Frankl called it, in which clarity is valuable even when it cannot fully free us—in which awareness may require first acknowledging our commitment to unawareness and plowing ahead anyway. More cheerfully sanguine schools of therapy exist, to be sure, especially in the Anglo-American tradition, and more politically radical readings of Freud have proliferated at least since the Frankfurt School. There is also the Jungian tradition, the Lacanian strain, and every other form and flavor of analysis, but these approaches fall outside the present focus. The concern here is with probing the mind of Freud himself, understood, in Rieff’s words, as he “derives lessons on the right conduct of life from the misery of living it.”

In Freud’s own vision, the psyche wasn’t built for bliss but for something more equivocal—ordinary unhappiness, famously, as an alternative to hysterical misery (as averred in his Studies on Hysteria). The practical aim was realistic but in its way demanding: that a person might after analysis be able to love and to work, lieben und arbeiten. Psychoanalysis does not cure, as the saying goes; it merely reconciles. Many of the Viennese analyst’s loudest detractors have gotten this backwards. The Freudian goal was not for the patient to unleash the id tout court, but for him to be able to sublimate knowingly—to negotiate a wary truce with the self and to become capable of his own depths. His more heretical students, those who chafed at his emotional conservatism, grasped him better than the critics who falsely caricatured him as a champion of unbridled instinct. In fact, Freud is often, and justly, described as both conservative and radical. He held that human beings could grow, could be happier, could remake our lives, but within limits; he unmasked our pieties and exploded our taboos, but he took seriously their protective function.

Sublimation—the rerouting of unruly drives into forms of work, love, art, and culture—is for Freud the miracle of civilization. It is the process through which conflict becomes achievement and through which anything worthwhile in human life is made. Neurosis and creation, in other words, spring from the same soil. Freud’s famous episode in Beyond the Pleasure Principle lays this bare: the child’s “fort…da!” game—throwing a toy away (“gone!”) and retrieving it (“there!”)—stages his mother’s absence and return in ritual form. Imagination does not restore what is missing, in the Freudian picture, but it is capable of formalizing missing-ness—of creatively accommodating a painful absence and making it generative. The main difference between the artist and the neurotic, in Lionel Trilling’s reading, is that “the poet is in command of his fantasy, while it is exactly the mark of the neurotic that he is possessed by his fantasy.” If all art-making is continuous with the mind’s basic operations, including its evasions—growing from the same roots as the dream, the slip of the tongue, and the symptom—then those who cast Freud as an enemy of sublimation miss the point in more ways than one. For Freud, the careful, deliberate redirection of raw psychic material into form is not some sort of glitch but a basic principle of life, for artist and ordinary person alike.

Freud, For and Against

The non-clinical, lay-intellectual landscape is today split between those who continue to mine Freud for such insights, however ambivalently, and those who treat him with visceral contempt. His fiercest antagonists generally reject him in one of two ways. Some object along long-standing scientific lines—the old Karl Popper charge of unfalsifiability, reinforced by the accurate assertion that Freud regarded himself as a neurologist, authored case studies, and so on (though the extent of that discrediting is often overstated, as the durable structure of psychodynamic therapy and recent overtures in neuroscience suggest). Others protest on ideological grounds, treating the investigation of unconscious life as itself frivolous or morally suspect. On the other side stand readers in comparative-literature departments, where he holds a central place even as his limitations are rigorously scrutinized, the post-pandemic Freud revivalists writing in magazines like Parapraxis or speaking on podcasts like Ordinary Unhappiness, and the seemingly increasing number of metropolitan creatives pursuing analytic training. Hence the claim that “Freud is enjoying something of a comeback,” heralded by a 2023 New York Times piece called “Not Your Daddy’s Freud.” But if he is really back, it is only at these margins. The chasm between those who take him seriously and those who write him off entirely has never felt wider.

Meanwhile, the standard conservative case against Freud—that he is desacralizing, preoccupied with sexuality, responsible for individualism as we know it—persists with ever-refreshed vigor, and now exists alongside something more peculiar. A psychosexually overdetermined fringe culture has emerged, one that loudly repudiates therapeutic introspection while theatrically parading its own complexes. A dazzling array of free-floating libidinal material gets displayed: the exuberant homoeroticism of Bronze Age Pervert; the fetishized submission of the “trad wife”; the paranoid machismo of the manosphere, where figures like Andrew Tate proclaim with straight faces that enjoying sex with women is “gay.” The contradictions and neuroses are performed proudly, as if to say, “You cannot psychoanalyze me—my underlying conflicts are too conspicuous, too militantly unexamined, too ironized.” In this way the Internet is flooded with shallow psychology jargon on one end and hyper-stylized bombast on the other—trading the proverbial barbs of “go to therapy” and “go to the gym” among themselves, as though one couldn’t do both—and defenses harden all around. 

While psychoanalysis reverts to its status as an esoteric language spoken among initiates for whom “Freud is back,” much of public life seems deprived of the tools he offered. We are the poorer for it. The common reader should turn to Freud for the same reasons we turn to Shakespeare or George Eliot: because his frameworks give shape and grammar to our experience, because he narrates something we could only otherwise narrate poorly or not at all. But we should also insist on reading him as an analyst. Freud tells us, without condescension, that our operating systems are defined by ambivalence, that we cannot eliminate contradiction but can fashion it into something livable, that we are creative and defensive creatures whose evasions are themselves imaginative acts. He tells us we will cling to suffering long after it stops serving us, that lucidity is always partial but is worth pursuing, and that, whether or not we narrate them accurately, we are responsible for our lives. The depthless cacophony of the digital condition cries out for more of him, not less.
